Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Augustus Mensah was seventy-two years old, a retired Coast Guard chief who had spent thirty-four years on the water, and he could still feel the hum of a boat engine in his bones. The toxic chemical exposure had happened on a routine inspection in the Gulf, a corroded valve on a cargo vessel that had leaked a fine, oily mist into the air before anyone noticed. He had been the one closest to it, the one who had to stay and seal the breach while the others backed away. He remembered the smell—sharp and sweet, like burnt almonds and gasoline—and the way it had clung to his uniform for days afterward. The memory came back to him now not as a story he told, but as a film that played over and over, a sequence he could not stop. When it played, he saw the exact grain of the metal grate beneath his boots, the precise angle of sunlight through the porthole, the way the chemical had beaded on his forearm like sweat. It was photographic, each frame frozen and perfectly detailed, and when the memory returned he felt so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing—once, mid-sentence at the dinner table, he had simply put down his fork and stared at the wall until his wife touched his arm.

The silence that followed those episodes became its own kind of threat. He had come to believe that unusual silence meant something dangerous was about to happen. At home, in the house he had shared with his wife for forty years, he felt on guard even inside his own living room. He would catch himself listening to the hum of the refrigerator, the creak of floorboards, and his body would respond before his mind caught up—his heart hammering, his palms wet, a tightness in his chest that made him think he was having a heart attack. He had strong physical reactions when something reminded him of the stressful experience, and almost everything reminded him. The smell of cleaning products at the grocery store. The sight of a yellow hazmat suit in a television show. The sound of a ship's horn drifting up from the harbor, three miles from his front door.

He had come to believe that he could not deal with even the slightest upset. A misplaced set of keys could send him into a spiral of irritability that lasted hours. If he thought about the event, he was certain he would not be able to handle it, so he pushed the memories away as soon as they surfaced—but pushing them away only made the film play faster when it returned. He had started avoiding the harbor entirely, taking the long way to the hardware store, telling his wife he no longer enjoyed the ocean air. His retirement had been built around fishing trips and boat maintenance; now he stayed inside, watching television with the volume turned up to fill the silence. The world, he had concluded, was a dangerous place. Not just the chemical, not just the cargo ship, but everything—the mailman's knock, the unexpected phone call, the quiet hour between midnight and dawn. He had stopped answering the door. He had stopped attending church. His wife had begun to cry during their arguments, asking where her husband had gone, and he had no answer for her.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in late November when he found himself standing in his own kitchen, unable to move, because the coffee maker had finished brewing and the sudden silence after the gurgling had stopped felt like a held breath before a disaster. He stood there for twenty minutes, his hand on the counter, waiting for something that never came. His wife found him and drove him to the VA clinic. He was afraid of what the memories would do to him if he let them in, but he was also afraid of what the silence was doing to the life he had left. He wanted to sit in his own living room without listening for a threat. He wanted to walk past the harbor without his chest seizing. He wanted, more than anything, to stop being afraid of the quiet.
